deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivations. It is the table of contents ('Inhalt') of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe'. The work was written in 1853/54 and published posthumously by Dedekind in 1867 (Abh. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 13). The page numbers refer to this fair copy (S. 4–41). The structure is as follows.

(A) History of the question whether a function can be represented by a trigonometric series:
- §1 From Euler to Fourier: the question arose in the 1753 dispute over the scope of d'Alembert's and Daniel Bernoulli's solutions of the vibrating-string problem; views of Euler, d'Alembert and Lagrange (p. 4).
- §2 From Fourier to Dirichlet: Fourier's correct view, opposed by Lagrange, 1807; Cauchy, 1826 (p. 10).
- §3 Since Dirichlet: Dirichlet settled the question in 1829 for the functions that occur in nature; Dirksen and Bessel, 1839 (p. 14).

(B) On the concept of a definite integral and the extent of its validity:
- §4 Definition of the definite integral (p. 19). In modern terms this is the Riemann integral as a limit of sums Σ δ_i f(x_{i-1}+ε_i δ_i).
- §5 Conditions for the integral to exist (p. 21). This is the oscillation criterion: Σ D_i δ_i → 0, equivalently for each σ the total length of intervals with oscillation > σ can be made arbitrarily small.
- §6 Special cases (p. 23). In the printed text this includes integrable functions with a dense set of discontinuities, e.g. Σ (nx)/n².

(C) Investigation of representability without special assumptions on the function:
- §7 Plan of the investigation (p. 27).
- Part I covers series whose coefficients ultimately become infinitely small.
  - §8 proves auxiliary theorems (p. 28). These are Riemann's method via the twice-integrated series F(x) = C + C'x − Σ A_n/n², his first and second lemmas on the symmetric second difference quotient Δ²F(x,α)/(4α²) and on Δ²F/(4α) → 0, and the localization principle.
  - §9 gives conditions for representability by a trigonometric series with coefficients tending to zero (p. 33).
  - §10 shows that the Fourier coefficients tend to zero when the function is bounded and integrable (p. 35). This is the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma for Riemann-integrable functions.
- Part II covers series whose coefficients do not decrease to zero. §11 reduces this case to the previous one (p. 37).
- Special cases: §12 treats functions without infinitely many maxima and minima (p. 39); §13 treats functions with infinitely many maxima and minima (p. 41).

The page shows the same structure as the following folio (another fair copy of the contents), with minor wording variants.

results.what: Definition of the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums (§4 announced)
Necessary and sufficient oscillation condition for integrability (§5 announced)
Fourier coefficients of a bounded integrable function tend to zero (§10 announced)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1854; Lebesgue 1903 for the Lebesgue-integrable case

results.what: Auxiliary theorems on trigonometric series with coefficients tending to zero, via the twice-integrated series (§8–9 announced)
results.modern_name: Riemann's first and second lemmas, Riemann localization principle

results.what: Historical periodization: vibrating-string controversy 1753, Fourier 1807, Cauchy 1826, Dirichlet 1829, Dirksen and Bessel 1839
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's historical introduction to the Habilitationsschrift

deep.surprise_reason: This is simply the table of contents of Riemann's well-known, published Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series. Its structure matches the printed 1867 text, and it contains no mathematics beyond section titles.

checkable.asserts: Illustrative only: the Fourier sine coefficient integral of x on [0,pi] for n=5 is pi/5 (generally -pi*cos(n*pi)/n), which tends to 0 as n grows, consistent with the §10 claim (Riemann–Lebesgue).
Illustrative only: the oscillatory integral of sin(nx) over [0,1] is (1-cos n)/n, whose limit as n→oo is 0.

transcription_corrections: The marker transcribed '{+I.+}' before '§. 7. Plan der Untersuchung' is a Roman 'I.' with a small insertion caret above it. The next page has the same 'I.' before §7.
The stray '3' after the heading 'Über den Begriff eines bestimmten Integrals...' and the '3' below the heading 'Untersuchung der Darstellbarkeit...' are faint marginal pencil marks, not page numbers.
The page reference for §1 reads 'S. 4' in the image.

Wording differs from the next folio: §10 here reads 'durchgehends endlich bleibt und eine Integration zulässt' versus 'endlich und einer Integration fähig ist' there. Part II here reads 'mit nicht ins Unendliche abnehmenden Coefficienten', while the next page's uncertain reading is 'ohne Voraussetzung über die Coefficienten'. The special-cases heading here reads 'Betrachtung besonderer Fälle' versus 'Untersuchung besonderer Fälle' there.
The main title here lacks 'willkürlich gegebenen', which appears on the next page's version: 'Geschichte der Frage über die Darstellbarkeit einer willkürlich gegebenen Function'.
